newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma black market petrol prices rise again.
newsitem.headline: Burma black market petrol prices rise again.

text.p: Burma's black market petrol prices, steady since a sudden leap in mid-September, have jumped again despite moves by the military government to keep them in check, residents said on Thursday.
Rumours were spreading that the government was unable to find new suppliers of crude oil, residents said, but local analysts blamed the price rise on an increase in demand and stiff rationing.

Petrol in Rangoon was selling on Thursday for about 320 kyats per gallon on the black market, the main supply source for most private vehicles, compared with an average of about 250 kyats per gallon over the last six weeks.
Supplies for the black market come from rations sold by civil servants seeking to boost their meagre wages, according to industry sources.
Although selling fuel in the black market is illegal the government has traditionally turned a blind eye.
Private car owners often have to rely on the black market to top up their tanks as most are only allowed to buy two gallons of petrol a week at the official price of 25 kyats per gallon.
Some with special coupons can buy an additional five gallons but must pay at a much higher rate.
Analysts said demand had increased following the end of the rainy season and further government limits on fuel rations.
A senior official in the Ministry of Energy told Reuters the ministry was currently negotiating crude supplies with various potential suppliers.

"We invited about five companies and have been discussing with them the supply of sweet crude for our refineries, without pre-fixing any terms and conditions," he said. The bidders were mostly Japanese firms.

Official media said earlier this week the government was also trying to boost its crude oil production at some onshore oil fields and to set up joint-ventures with foreign companies with the aim to increase oil production.
It said the ministry was also importing fuel from various unidentified sources on a grace period basis.
The ministry official said Burma's current domestic crude production was 12,000 barrels per day (bpd), down from 35,000 bpd in 1982.
In mid-September petrol prices jumped to about 400-420 kyats per gallon on panic buying as consumers feared a shortage on rumours that a foreign firm had stopped supplying crude to Burma.
Japan's Mitsui & Co Ltd, a key supplier, said in September Rangoon was behind in some of its payments for crude oil and diesel fuel sold under annual term contracts.

The company said it believed the delay was due to operational matters like issuing letters of credit. It said Mitsui had fulfilled all obligations on its term contract which expired on September 7, including cargo loadings.
The government at the time denied a fuel shortage and took measures to improve distribution from filling stations. Prices then dropped to about 250 kyats per gallon.
